items: Prime Minister of Mauritius from 1968 to 1982
books: Sir Seewoosagur Ramgoolam GCMG (18 September 1900 – 15 December 1985), often known as SSR or Chacha ("uncle"), was a Mauritian physician and statesman who led Mauritius to independence from the United Kingdom. He was the colony's chief minister from 1961 and premier from 1964, the first prime minister of independent Mauritius from 1968 to 1982, and governor-general from 1983 until his death. He is widely known in Mauritius as the "Father of the Nation".

The son of an indentured labourer from Bihar, Ramgoolam was born in a village in eastern Mauritius. He studied medicine in London, where he joined the Fabian Society and Indian nationalist circles and met Mahatma Gandhi. After returning home in 1935 he became a leader of the Indo-Mauritian community, co-founded the newspaper Advance and was nominated to the colony's Council of Government in 1940. Elected to the Legislative Council in 1948, he became the leader of the Labour Party group in the council and, by 1958, of the party itself. He campaigned for universal suffrage and ministerial government, both of which Britain conceded in the late 1950s.

As chief minister and premier, Ramgoolam led the parties that sought independence at the Lancaster House conference of 1965. During the conference, after being told that Britain could separate the islands without Mauritian consent, he agreed to the detachment of the Chagos Archipelago, which Britain made into the British Indian Ocean Territory. The detachment led to the expulsion of the islands' inhabitants between 1967 and 1973, a decision taken by the United Kingdom and the United States, not by Mauritius. Opponents, and some of the displaced Chagossians, long accused Ramgoolam of trading the islands for independence. British records later showed that Britain was prepared to detach them regardless, and in 2019 the International Court of Justice found that the detachment had not been based on the free and genuine will of the people of Mauritius.

Sir Anerood Jugnauth GCSK KCMG PC QC (29 March 1930 – 3 June 2021) was a Mauritian statesman, barrister, and politician. He served six terms as Prime Minister, two terms as President and one term as Leader of Opposition. Often called the father of the Mauritian economic miracle, he led Mauritius through unprecedented economic growth and modernization as both Prime Minister and President.
He diversified the economy beyond sugarcane into tourism, textiles, offshore services, IT, and knowledge sectors, while modernizing infrastructure like airports, ports, and roads.
Under his leadership, Mauritius became a republic on 12 March 1992, improved living standards, expanded social welfare, and secured UNESCO World Heritage Sites. He also championed Mauritius’s sovereignty over the Chagos Archipelago internationally, leaving a legacy of economic prosperity and political stability for the country.

Navinchandra Ramgoolam (born 14 July 1947) is a Mauritian politician, physician and barrister who has been Prime Minister of Mauritius since November 2024, an office he previously held from 1995 to 2000 and from 2005 to 2014. He has led the Labour Party since 1991 and has also been Minister of Finance since 2024. The son of Seewoosagur Ramgoolam, who led Mauritius to independence in 1968 and was its first prime minister, he trained as a doctor in Dublin and worked in hospitals in Ireland, England and Mauritius before reading law at the London School of Economics and being called to the bar in 1993.

Ramgoolam became Labour's leader and Leader of the Opposition in 1991. In alliance with Paul Bérenger's Mauritian Militant Movement (MMM), Labour won every seat on the island of Mauritius at the 1995 general election. His first government replaced the sales tax with value-added tax, legislated against domestic violence and for a national human rights commission, provided for private broadcasting and hosted the launch of the Indian Ocean Rim Association, while the economy grew by an average of more than five per cent a year. The coalition with the MMM ended in 1997, the riots that followed the death in police custody of the singer Kaya tested the government in 1999, and Labour was heavily defeated by an alliance of the Militant Socialist Movement (MSM) and the MMM in 2000.

Returning to power in 2005 at the head of the Alliance Sociale, Ramgoolam governed through the loss of preferential access for Mauritian textiles and sugar. His finance minister, Rama Sithanen, replaced a complex tax system with a flat rate of 15 per cent, abolished most investment-incentive schemes, opened the economy to foreign investors and skilled workers and restructured the sugar industry, reforms that the International Monetary Fund (IMF) commended.
